clue.text: As ref says, I had characters playing who were not a bit tired

definitions.text: who were not a bit tired
definitions.note: a relative clause standing for an adjectival phrase describing people

indicators.note: the letters are made to play about, so they move into a new order

parts.note: 'characters' tells you to use these letters as written

explanation.surface: Players quote the referee, insisting they never felt the slightest fatigue during the match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters' just means the letters of 'I had' join those of 'As ref says' in the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone full of energy and not weary at all, which is how people who were not tired would be described.

clue.text: Make a formal ceremony of boxer in America entering office

indicators.note: the boxer sits inside the letters for America
the combined piece goes into the word for office, splitting it

parts.note: first part of RITE, a religious office or service
Muhammad Ali, the crossword's favourite boxer

explanation.surface: A boxer takes a job in an American office, and the routine becomes a ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: Office here is the church sense, a rite or set form of service, and it wraps around everything else.
explanation.definitionFit: To ritualise something is to turn it into a ritual, a fixed formal ceremony.

clue.text: Pudding and a packet of fags appealing to Will?

parts.note: cigarettes (fags in British slang) are commonly sold in packs of twenty

explanation.surface: A dessert and some cigarettes, offered as treats to someone called Will.
explanation.walkthrough: Will is Shakespeare: 'Then come kiss me, sweet and twenty' is from a song in Twelfth Night. Fags is British slang for cigarettes.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare used the phrase for a young and attractive person, so it describes what Will found appealing; the question mark flags the playful pointer.

clue.text: Unsavoury character not welcome at Sotheby's?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a dishonest or disreputable person
second meaning, read literally: a poor item put up for sale at an auction house

explanation.surface: A shady person gets turned away from a smart London auction house.
explanation.walkthrough: Sotheby's is a famous auction house, where the things for sale are called lots.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for a rogue doubles as a literal description of a poor-quality item offered at auction.

clue.text: Finished swopping parts of working gear

indicators.note: the two halves of the word trade places, front going to the back

explanation.surface: Someone has finished work after changing pieces of their kit.
explanation.definitionFit: When something is all over it has ended, the same as being finished.

clue.text: Posh fruit squeezed by an android, possibly

indicators.note: squeezed means held tightly between two other letters

parts.note: first letter of the word taken as written
botanically a tomato is a fruit
end of the word taken as written

explanation.surface: An upmarket piece of fruit is being crushed by a robot.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class (as opposed to non-U) is a British convention; U plus TOMATO sits inside AN.
explanation.definitionFit: An android is a humanlike robot, one example of a self-operating machine; 'possibly' marks it as an example.

clue.text: A kind of lobster that's short and thick

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the ... lobster, a small crustacean
second meaning: stocky, dumpy in shape

explanation.surface: Describing a lobster species as stubby and chunky.
explanation.definitionFit: Squat lobsters are a group of crustaceans, and squat as an adjective means low, broad and stocky.

clue.text: Tree trunk clutched by heroin addict?

indicators.note: the trunk is held inside, between the two parts of the drug user

parts.note: the trunk of the body, or a large box
a nut is an enthusiast or fanatic

explanation.surface: A junkie clinging to the trunk of a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tree trunk' reads as one thing, but Tree is the definition and trunk is a separate piece held by the two words that follow.
explanation.definitionFit: The horse chestnut is a large tree whose seeds British children call conkers.

clue.text: Ancient historian looking after students in digs

definitions.text: Ancient historian looking after students in digs

parts.words: Ancient historian looking after students in digs
parts.note: surface reading: an elderly history don acting as landlord to students in their lodgings
setter's reading: digs are excavations, and the historian studies ancient times, supervising students on site

explanation.surface: An old history teacher who keeps an eye on students in their rented rooms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ancient' seems to describe the historian's age; it really describes what they study. Digs is British slang for lodgings.
explanation.definitionFit: This kind of scientist studies the ancient past by excavating sites, often supervising student volunteers at digs.

clue.text: Attentive man at dance not involved at first

indicators.note: involved means tangled up, so the letters are twisted round

parts.note: a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: A man at a dance who isn't joining in, yet is paying close attention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' looks like a negative attached to 'involved', but it is the anagram fodder, and 'at first' places it at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on the ball is an idiom for being alert and quick to respond.

clue.text: Faster game occupies three quarters of school session

indicators.note: keeping three of four letters means the last is dropped
the game takes up residence inside the shortened session

parts.note: first three of the four letters of TERM

explanation.surface: A quicker game fills most of the school term.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Faster' looks like speed, but fast here means firm and loyal, as in fast friends.
explanation.definitionFit: Fast in the sense of steadfast or firmly fixed is close to true, faithful; truer means more loyal.

clue.text: Slight stir in street

indicators.note: the prison word is placed inside the abbreviation for street

parts.note: stir and can are both slang for prison

explanation.surface: A small commotion breaks out on the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stir' suggests a commotion, but it is slang for jail, as is can.
explanation.definitionFit: Scant and slight both mean barely sufficient, very little in amount.

clue.text: Close engagement? Not at Wimbledon, apparently

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a marriage based on affection, an intimate betrothal
second meaning: in tennis love is nil, so the name suggests a one-sided game, the very opposite of close

explanation.surface: A tense, tightly fought encounter, but not on the courts of the famous tennis tournament.
explanation.walkthrough: Wimbledon is the London tennis championship, where 'love' means a score of nil.
explanation.definitionFit: A marriage made for affection rather than money is an engagement of close hearts, while in tennis terms the phrase sounds anything but close.

clue.text: Having more than one graphic section appended to chapter 51

indicators.note: appended means tacked on after, so this piece follows the others

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for chapter

explanation.surface: A book's fifty-first chapter gets an extra section full of illustrations.
explanation.definitionFit: Clip art is a stock collection of ready-made pictures, a plural idea though the word is singular.

clue.text: See 3
Gunners find relentless competition

parts.note: to trace something is to track it down

explanation.surface: Soldiers discover that life is one endless contest.
explanation.walkthrough: Gunners is the usual crossword pointer to RA, the British Army's Royal Artillery.
explanation.definitionFit: The rat race is the idiom for the exhausting, endless struggle for success in work and life.

clue.text: How much came to Berlin from stolen melody?

explanation.surface: Asking how much of a pinched tune reached a German city.
explanation.walkthrough: In 1948–49 West Berlin was supplied by air during the Soviet blockade, the Berlin Airlift.
explanation.definitionFit: Supplies were flown into the blockaded city, so much of what arrived there was carried by aircraft in the historic airlift.

clue.text: Revised defective deed to include workers

indicators.note: the workers are taken inside the rearranged letters
something defective is faulty, so the letters are put wrongly in order

parts.note: men are workers, as in management and men

explanation.surface: A flawed legal document was rewritten to bring in the employees.
explanation.definitionFit: To emend a text is to correct it, so an emended document has been revised.

clue.text: Expressionless god, deceased

parts.note: Pan, the Greek god of the wild

explanation.surface: A dead deity with a blank face.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces are taken in reverse of the clue's order: the word for deceased comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadpan face or delivery shows no emotion, the same as being expressionless.

clue.text: Goal welcomed by endless song — it's catching on

indicators.note: without an end, so the final letter is cut off
being welcomed in means being taken inside

parts.note: a trill is a warbling song, here missing its last letter

explanation.surface: A goal greeted by a never-ending chant: the fashion is spreading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'catching on' sounds like a craze becoming popular; here it means literally grabbing hold.
explanation.definitionFit: A tendril is the thin coiling shoot a climbing plant uses to grip and attach itself to supports.

clue.text: Bolt shed

explanation.walkthrough: Both words look like nouns, a lock and a garden building, but both are verbs.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking off can mean leaving in a hurry, and taking off clothing means shedding it.

clue.text: Return to earlier form upset footballer

parts.note: to throw someone is to disconcert them
a back is a defensive player

explanation.surface: A player who rediscovers old form after being knocked off balance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return' is a noun here, matching the noun answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A throwback is a reversion to an earlier type or style, a return to a former form.

clue.text: Apostate bishop taking part in dance

indicators.note: the bishop joins the dance by stepping inside it

parts.note: a reel is a Scottish dance

explanation.surface: A cleric who has abandoned the faith joins in a dance.
explanation.definitionFit: An apostate renounces a belief or allegiance, and a rebel likewise defies the established cause.

clue.text: Coupling's tiresome when Romeo's stricken

indicators.note: struck out means removed, so the letter for this name goes

parts.note: R is Romeo in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: Romance becomes a chore once the lover falls ill.
explanation.definitionFit: Coupling as a verb means joining together, the same as tying.

clue.text: Tenth article contains it

indicators.note: the article holds the other word inside it

explanation.surface: A tenth item in a list is said to hold something.
explanation.definitionFit: A tithe was a tenth of produce or income paid to the church, so the word names a tenth part.

clue.text: No time for headgear in town

definitions.note: a phrase standing for an adjective meaning belonging to a town

indicators.note: having no time means the letter for time is removed

explanation.surface: No time to buy a hat while in the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Urban describes things situated in a town or city rather than the countryside.

clue.text: Expert says they can cause problems for older men

definitions.text: they can cause problems for older men

explanation.surface: A specialist warns of something that troubles elderly men.
explanation.definitionFit: The prostate gland commonly enlarges with age, giving many older men urinary and other medical problems.

clue.text: Green areas acting as WC?

parts.note: W. C. Fields was an American comic actor; acting as him means playing Fields

explanation.surface: Grassy spaces being used as public toilets.
explanation.walkthrough: WC looks like a lavatory; it is W. C. Fields, the comedian, so an actor portraying him is playing Fields.
explanation.definitionFit: Playing fields are grassed open spaces set aside for sport and games.
